meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.
Spelled في in casual Levantine writing and negated directly with ما (ما في مكان 'there is no place', ما في حدا 'nobody is here').

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
There is no time right now.

meanings.note: With possessive -ي: مكاني ('my place / my spot').
Spoken Levantine pronunciation of ثاني (taani); feminine الثانية means 'the other / the next'.

examples.trans: I sat in the second row.

meanings.note: High-frequency Jordanian word for 'like': زي هيك ('like this') and زي هاد المكان ('like this place').
Everyday Jordanian masculine demonstrative used before a definite noun (هاد الإشي، هاد الحكي) or as a pronoun (حتى لو هاد آخر إشي).
Invariable modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (لازم نتحمل، مش لازم نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: We have to go to class now.

meanings.note: Feminine counterpart of الواحد when speaking generically about a girl or woman (لازم الوحدة تشوفه بعينها).

examples.trans: A girl has to stand up for herself.
Each one of us has a role.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.

meanings.note: Idiomatic in شفت بعيني / بعينها ('saw with my/her own eyes') and بتشوفه العين ('the eye sees').

examples.trans: I saw what happened with my own eyes.

examples.text: مش كل إشي بتشوفه العين صح.
examples.trans: Not everything the eye sees is true.

meanings.note: Used before nouns (قبل بوقت 'ahead of time'), before ما + verb (قبل ما تعصب 'before she gets angry'), or alone at the end of a clause ('beforehand').

examples.trans: I arrived at school before the bell.

meanings.note: Used in قبل ما تحكم ('before she judges').

examples.trans: Hear the story before you judge.

meanings.note: Unvocalized اطلعي in Jordanian speech represents it-talla'i ('look over there!').

examples.trans: Look over there by the gate.
She looked at me without speaking.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker or back to the scene of an event (كنتي هناك 'you were there').

examples.trans: Look over there by the tree.
We have to be there on time.

meanings.note: Expresses location (عند باب الساحة), movement toward someone with لـ (لعندي 'up to me'), and possession (عندي وقت 'I have time', عنا 'we have').

examples.trans: Come over to me for a moment.

meanings.note: Used for room doors and outdoor school gates (باب الساحة 'the courtyard gate').

examples.trans: Wait for me at the school gate.

meanings.note: At AlRawabi, الساحة is the central open courtyard where students gather.

examples.trans: We went down to the courtyard at recess.
The girls are standing in the middle of the courtyard.

meanings.note: Active participle of وقف used for present posture (ليان واقفة، أنا واقفة بمكاني).

examples.trans: Why are you standing by the door?
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').
With كـ + الـ, كالعادة means 'as usual'.

examples.trans: I have a habit of reading before sleep.

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine pronunciation (daayman) of classical دائماً.
Active participle of مشى: ماشيين وراها ('walking behind her / following her lead').

examples.trans: We were walking in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Spoken form of وراء: spatial 'behind' (ماشيين وراها، من ورا 'from behind') and sequential 'one after another' (واحدة ورا الثانية).

examples.trans: I sat at the desk behind you.
They walked into class one after another.

meanings.note: Central setting: مدرسة الروابي للبنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls').

examples.trans: The school is close to our house.
I like going to school early.

meanings.note: Emphasizes contrast in cleft sentences like هي اللي بلشت ('she is the one who started it').

examples.trans: She has been my friend since childhood.

meanings.note: Intransitive 'move': ما بتتحرك خطوة بدونهم ('she doesn't move a step without them').
Used both literally ('walk a step') and figuratively (معكم بكل خطوة 'with you in every step').

examples.trans: I'm with you every step of the way.

meanings.note: Takes nouns or pronoun suffixes directly (بدونهم 'without them').

examples.trans: I solved the question without help.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').
Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (formal هنا).

examples.trans: Come sit here next to me.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine form of نصف (nuss): بنص الساحة means 'in the middle of the courtyard'.

examples.trans: Don't stand in the middle of the path.

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.

meanings.note: Active participle of راح; كنا رايحين عالصف means 'we were on our way to class'.

examples.trans: We were heading to the principal.

meanings.note: عالصف contracts على الصف ('to class'), and بالصف means 'in class'.

examples.trans: Go back to class right now.
We are in the same class.

meanings.note: High-frequency Levantine word for 'now' (contracted from هاد الوقت).

examples.trans: We have to go to class right now.
I feel a bit relieved now.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.
Standard Jordanian private-school address for a female teacher or principal, used alone (يا مس) or before her first name (مس فاتن، مس عبير).

examples.trans: Ms. Faten is in her office now.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine singular demonstrative (هاي مدرسة الروابي، هاي أول مرة).
Placed before a noun for 'first' (أول مرة), or at the end of a clause adverbially for 'first / beforehand' (نخلصه أول).

examples.trans: This is the first time I see you here.

meanings.note: Placed directly before an indefinite singular noun (آخر مرة 'the last time', آخر إشي 'the last thing') without changing for gender.

examples.trans: This is the last thing I have.

meanings.note: Appears in المرة الجاي ('next time'), أول وآخر مرة ('first and last time'), بالمرة ('at all'), and plural مرات ('sometimes').

examples.trans: This is the first time I come here.
Sometimes we sit in the library.

meanings.note: Plural متأخرين is used in spoken Jordanian for both mixed and all-female groups (بشوفكم متأخرين).

examples.trans: Why are you always late to class?

meanings.note: Used alone or at the start of a reply to give warm reassurance or certainty.
In the polite Jordanian apology حقك علينا ('your right is upon us'), it means 'we're sorry / our fault'.
Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Derived from يا الله; urges action ('Come on, get off!') or wraps up warmly ('Alright, next time I'll come!').

examples.trans: Come on quickly, we'll be late!

meanings.note: Imperative plural ارجعوا عالصف ('go back to class!').
With بـ, بسرعة means 'quickly / right away'.
Invariable comparative/superlative adjective; أحسن إلنا means 'it is better for us'.

examples.trans: This way is better for everyone.
It's better that we go now.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).
Means 'go' (نروح 'we go'), and with على (راح علي إشي؟) forms the idiomatic Jordanian way to ask 'did I miss anything?'.

examples.trans: Come on, let's go to class.
I missed the bus this morning.

meanings.note: Form II intransitive Levantine verb ('assab): قبل ما تعصب ('before she gets mad').
Appears in the classic Arabic farewell مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!', literally 'with safety').
